about: The top four of five concepts after three judged rounds (6 Nov), best first. scores = the judge's final score for each of the 21 bet questions, in bet.json order (b1.f, b1.e, b1.i, b2.f ... b7.i), 0/1/2. sections = each section's number, title and the bet questions it answers (the concept's own claim). notes = the judge's round-3 notes, shown on the study page. Ours, not the client's.

options.name: Sotto Voce
options.premise: The page runs in two registers, like the deck: upright is the club's voice, a narrow italic margin is ours, talking about that work. Each section is a picture first, with at most one upright line and one italic aside.

sections.title: The cost of the wrong member
What it did, and what's out there now

options.notes: Strongest on fidelity: every one of his ideas is on the page and every quote checks out against 46. Fixes it suggests: merge §3's places bar into §1; §6 is overloaded (move the four thumbnails up beside §3); typeset §7's stickies rather than a board export (done here, for the public-repo rule); mark b3.i as our reading; keep the §0 money chip quiet; let §4's dominoes resolve into wanting.

options.name: Your Move
options.premise: The case study is a short game in three moves. At each one the reader decides first (which night, who the competition is, who to sign first) and our answer is the reveal. It ends by giving the reader a chair at the table and asking about their own Tuesday.

sections.title: Move two: who are they up against?
The six Tuesdays, and what we made
Move three: who do you sign first?
What happened, and what they carry now

options.notes: The best structural answer to 'the case study as a conversation', and the third chair is the best 'my kind of people' image. Fixes it suggests: fold Move two into Move one's reveal (three quizzes plus a closing ask reads like a game); §5 is the wordiest section on any page, keep the chain line and one guide line; one italic in §6; put two or three raw stickies on the §7 table for 'something tender'; let §1's block be wordless; settle the tag's time.

options.name: Two Tuesdays
options.premise: The page draws the same Tuesday twice: as it was (value they couldn't break down, the wrong members, no money in hand) and as it turned out (the right members, 88% signed faster than expected, a club that opened in our words). Italic is us, roman is only ever the client's sourced words.

sections.title: The slab, the hinge, and what we made
Why a Tuesday: predict, then reveal
The cost, as dominoes: you choose the first one
What it did: 88%, and a club that opened in our words
The case study asks back, once, plus the tag

options.notes: The strongest visuals: the hinge, choosing the first domino, the live site. Its one rule break (a line on the §6 cards that traces only to Study 83) is fixed here: the cards are the founders' own Tuesday answers from Study 46. Also done here: hover cards without income, a silhouette instead of a member name on the chip, b3.i marked as our reading. Still open: the hero holds too much; §7 asks 'where would you have started?' where he said 'would you have solved it that way?'; roman is nearly absent.

options.name: Tuesday to Tuesday
options.premise: One week, from a Tuesday with nothing in it to the next Tuesday, which has the club in it. It opens by asking the reader to pick the night and closes by asking how they'd have solved it. The pictures carry the 21 answers; the words are labels and two voices.

sections.title: I want those two in the room
Would you have solved it that way?

options.notes: The cleanest and least wordy page. Its structural bug: §0 already labels every night, then §1 asks which night, so the answer comes before the question. Fixes it suggests: leave §0's nights dark and unlabelled; show the competition once (drop the places ribbon, keep §3's slot); one domino row plus a switch instead of three animations; say in one italic line that the margin voice is these two; let one aside be funny; show the tag on the first screen too.
